summary.text: Take \(n=0\). Then \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\), while for every \(k>1\), \(\Phi_k(0)=1\) because the constant term of the \(k\)-th cyclotomic polynomial is \(1\); hence the absolute value is always \(1\), which is not prime.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\Phi_k(X)\) denote the \(k\)-th cyclotomic polynomial, and let \(|m|\) denote the ordinary absolute value of an integer \(m\). Consider the assertion as it is formally quantified: for every natural number \(n\), including \(0\), there is a positive integer \(k\) for which \(|\Phi_k(n)|\) is prime. We show that \(n=0\) is a counterexample.

We first record the constant terms of the cyclotomic polynomials. For \(k=1\),
\[
\Phi_1(X)=X-1,
\]
so
\[
\Phi_1(0)=-1.
\]
For every \(k>1\), one has
\[
\Phi_k(0)=1.
\]
Here is a direct justification of the latter standard fact. For \(k=2\), \(\Phi_2(X)=X+1\), so the result is immediate. Now suppose \(k>2\), and let \(\zeta\) be a primitive \(k\)-th root of unity. The roots of \(\Phi_k\) are precisely \(\zeta^j\), where \(1\leq j\leq k\) and \(\gcd(j,k)=1\). Hence its constant term is
\[
(-1)^{\varphi(k)}\zeta^S,
\qquad
S=\sum_{\substack{1\leq j\leq k\\ \gcd(j,k)=1}}j.
\]
When \(k>2\), the reduced residue classes pair as \(j\) and \(k-j\). There is no fixed point in this pairing: a fixed point would satisfy \(2j=k\), but then \(j=k/2\) would not be relatively prime to \(k\). Thus \(\varphi(k)\) is even, and each of the \(\varphi(k)/2\) pairs has sum \(k\). Consequently
\[
S=\frac{k\varphi(k)}2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\zeta^S=(\zeta^k)^{\varphi(k)/2}=1,
\]
and, because \(\varphi(k)\) is even, \((-1)^{\varphi(k)}=1\). Therefore \(\Phi_k(0)=1\), as claimed.

Assume, toward a contradiction, that the asserted universal existence statement holds. Applying it to the natural number \(n=0\), we obtain a positive integer \(k\) such that
\[
|\Phi_k(0)|
\]
is prime. There are two exhaustive cases.

First suppose \(k=1\). Then
\[
|\Phi_k(0)|=|\Phi_1(0)|=|-1|=1.
\]
But \(1\) is not prime, contradicting the required primality.

Now suppose \(k\neq1\). Since \(k\) is a positive integer, this implies \(k>1\). By the constant-term result proved above,
\[
\Phi_k(0)=1,
\]
and therefore
\[
|\Phi_k(0)|=1.
\]
Again, \(1\) is not prime, giving the same contradiction.

Thus no positive integer \(k\) makes \(|\Phi_k(0)|\) prime. Hence the statement
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists k>0:\ |\Phi_k(n)|\text{ is prime}
\]
is false when \(\mathbb N\) includes \(0\); its counterexample is \(n=0\).

There is an important domain qualification. The argument above is exactly a disproof of the formal statement, whose quantifier ranges over all natural numbers and therefore includes \(0\). If the canonical OEIS question is instead read literally as quantifying only over positive integers \(n\geq1\), then \(n=0\) lies outside its domain, and this argument does not disprove that positive-integer version. It establishes only that the formal all-natural-numbers formulation is false.
